questions.q: Why isn't a one-time, design-phase review of a data model sufficient on its own?
options: Because design-phase reviews are never accurate in the first place
Because it catches launch-time problems but not the drift that only appears after months of real production usage
Because Salesforce requires a review only once per org lifetime
Because design-phase reviews are only required for custom objects, not standard objects
questions.explain: A design-time review catches what's visible at launch. Problems like unused fields, relationship skew, and schema drift only become visible after real usage accumulates, which is exactly why a recurring review process is needed.

questions.q: A lookup relationship's child-record count per parent has grown far beyond what it was originally designed for. Which category of a structured data model review would catch this?
options: Automation load
Relationship health
Duplicate or overlapping objects
Unused fields and objects
questions.explain: Relationship health specifically checks whether a relationship's actual volume still matches what it was designed to handle, flagging skew risk before it becomes a production incident.

questions.q: Two teams have independently built custom objects that capture nearly the same concept without discovering each other's work. What should a data model review flag this as?
options: A governor-limit violation
A consolidation opportunity, under the duplicate or overlapping objects category
A storage-limit issue only
This is not something a data model review would catch
questions.explain: Independently-grown objects capturing near-identical concepts are a classic duplicate/overlapping-objects finding, and a review is specifically designed to surface these consolidation opportunities.

questions.q: How should a data model review's cadence typically be set?
options: At a fixed, identical interval for every org regardless of how much the schema is changing
Only once, at the time the org is first built
Scaled to the org's rate of change, with a mandatory review also triggered by major events like a merger or new business unit launch
Never on a schedule — only reactively, after a production incident occurs
questions.explain: Cadence should scale with how fast the org is changing — a fast-changing org needs more frequent reviews — and a major event like a merger or release should trigger a review outside the normal schedule rather than waiting for the next scheduled date.

questions.q: What makes a data model review's output actually useful rather than close to worthless?
options: Producing the longest possible list of observations
Running the review as infrequently as possible to save time
Each finding getting an assigned owner and a clear disposition (fix now, schedule later, or accept and document the risk)
Keeping the findings only in the reviewer's personal notes
questions.explain: A review that only documents observations without assigning ownership and a disposition to each finding tends to just re-discover the same issues at the next review with nothing having changed — the findings have to be actionable to justify the recurring process.
